name: Carla Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do interior fit-out for a shopfitting firm called Brightline. That means when a shop or a café or an office floor is an empty concrete box, we come in and build everything inside it: stud walls, drywall, ceilings, door frames, the counters sometimes. Most of our work is nights, because the shopping centre wants the shops open in the day, so I start at eight in the evening and finish at five in the morning. I love the moment the lights go on in a finished unit and it looks like a real place. What I hate is sleeping in the day and never seeing my girlfriend properly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about money and home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Priya, she's a nurse on a children's ward, so between her shifts and my nights we're like ships passing. Pay at Brightline is lower than the big firms because it's a small outfit, and there aren't many fit-out companies near us, so I can't just walk across the road to another job. We've got maybe three weeks of money saved. I use one of those AI chat tools now and then, mostly to check a building regulation or write a polite email to a site manager when I'm angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds about right for my job. Nobody's building a robot that can hang a ceiling at three in the morning in a shopping centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get back to talking about real problems, like pay and night work. With the women I know in the trade, there's a little group of us online, I'd probably say AI was a distraction from fair wages. I'd say it without being smug, though, because loads of people were genuinely scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means not much changes for me, and I'd be glad. Maybe the AI tool gets a bit better at helping me with quotes and regulations. But I'd still be on nights, still underpaid, still eyeing the job ads for something in the daytime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, really. I'd keep using the chat tool for the odd email and keep pushing Brightline for a day-shift rota. I'd probably join the union properly instead of just meaning to, because if nothing big changes then the old ways of getting a raise still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored by it, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you keep meaning to join the union. What's stopped you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fee, mostly, and the meetings are in the evening when I'm at work. My dad was a union man at the bus depot and he'd be ashamed of me. In this picture I'd finally just do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good night at work look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week we did a bakery in the east wing, curved counter, the owner cried when she saw it. Me and Tomasz had the ceiling up by two and we were laughing about something stupid. That's a good night.

S0.say: I'd say good, now let's talk about real problems like pay and night work. In my online group of women in the trade I'd call AI a distraction from fair wages, without being smug about it.
S0.think: Privately it means not much changes for me and I'd be glad. The AI tool might help a bit more with quotes, but I'd still be on nights and underpaid.
S0.do: Keeps working nights at Brightline, keeps using the chat tool for emails and regulations, and asks for a day-shift rota. Finally pays to join the union.
S0.quote: Nobody's building a robot that can hang a ceiling at three in the morning in a shopping centre.
S0.fieldNote: Carla treats this picture as a return to ordinary problems, mostly night shifts and pay. She already uses AI lightly and without fuss. Her father's union past clearly weighs on her, and joining is the one change she'd make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one I can actually picture. Like when everyone got smartphones and suddenly the site manager could message you at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers need a say in how it comes in. I'd post that in the group, and at work I'd tell the boss that if the drawings and measuring get faster, the time saved should go to us, not just to squeezing in another job. I'd try to say it calmly so I don't get labelled the difficult one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think fit-out is safer than a lot of jobs, because every shop is a different weird shape. But I've seen the videos of robots that print drywall layout lines on the floor, and the ones that fix ceiling boards. They wouldn't take my job, they'd take half of it, and half my wage with it maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of people at Brightline tried the new tools, then I'd learn them properly, the layout apps and the tablets with the 3D plans. I'd join the union and ask them to negotiate training. And I'd start saving, even a bit, because I don't want to be on three weeks of money when they cut hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I think I'd be okay. I'm usually in the second wave with new stuff and that's served me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're usually in the second wave. Give me an example.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When Brightline got a laser level that throws lines around the whole room, Tomasz grabbed it the first day. I watched him for a week, saw it actually saved time, then I asked him to show me. Now I won't work without it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray. He's fifty-something, he's been fitting ceilings since before I was born, and he hates his phone. If the job becomes half tablet, Ray's the one they'd push out, and he's got nothing else.

S1.say: I'd say workers need a say in how it comes in, and that time saved by faster drawings should go to us, not to squeezing in another job. I'd say it calmly so I'm not labelled the difficult one.
S1.think: Privately I think fit-out is safer than most jobs because every unit is a strange shape. But robots that mark layouts or fix boards could take half my work, and maybe half my wage.
S1.do: Learns the layout apps and 3D-plan tablets once colleagues have proved them, joins the union to push for training, and starts saving a little each week.
S1.feel: Uneasy but fairly confident, because waiting for the second wave has worked for her before.
S1.quote: They wouldn't take my job, they'd take half of it, and half my wage with it maybe.
S1.fieldNote: Carla has a clear, tested way of handling new tools: watch first, then learn. Her worry is losing hours rather than losing the job outright. She immediately thinks of an older colleague, Ray, who would struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Oh. That's not a work problem anymore, that's everything at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be handled by the government, full stop, because the companies won't do it. I'd say people need an income while this happens, and that the companies making the robots should be taxed to pay for it. I'd be at the protests with Priya, she'd be worried about the hospital too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd lose the job within a year of it arriving. Shopfitting is all about doing it fast and cheap at night, and a robot that never sleeps is exactly what a shopping centre would want. With three weeks of savings, I don't have a lot of ground to stand on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight away, no holidays, no new tools, and I'd sell my van because Priya and I could share her car. I'd go to the union and push hard, and I'd sign up for whatever support the government put in place, no shame. If I had a few months, I'd try for a job inspecting robot work on sites, someone has to sign it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. More scared than I thought I'd be when you started reading it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said someone has to sign it off. Do you really believe there'd be jobs like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, yeah, for a while. Building inspectors, safety checks, people who can tell when a wall's wrong. But how many? Maybe one for every ten of us. I'd be fighting Tomasz for it, and he's quicker with tech than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Priya talk about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether her job's safe, mostly, because it's the one keeping the rent paid. And whether we still try to have a baby in a few years. I think we'd go quiet on that one.

S2.say: I'd say the government has to handle this because companies won't, and that people need an income while it happens, paid by taxing the companies making the robots. I'd go to the protests with Priya.
S2.think: Privately I think I'd lose the job within a year, because a robot that never sleeps is exactly what a shopping centre wants for night fit-outs. With three weeks of savings I have little ground to stand on.
S2.do: Cuts all spending at once and sells her van to share Priya's car. Pushes the union, signs up for government support, and tries for a job checking robot work on sites.
S2.feel: Scared, more than she expected when the card was read out.
S2.quote: A robot that never sleeps is exactly what a shopping centre would want.
S2.fieldNote: The speed of this picture shifts Carla from her usual watch-and-learn approach to plain fear. She sees a narrow route into inspection work but doubts there are enough places. Her household now leans on Priya's nursing job, and a future baby goes quiet in the conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to finish a course, at least. That's the first thing I thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years and we'd better not waste them like we did with climate change. I'd push in the union for retraining money and for rules on how fast companies can bring robots in. I'd post about it, but more about solutions than doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me a real chance to get out ahead of it. I'd be thirty-two, and if I'd done a building inspection qualification by then, I'd be one of the people checking the robots' work instead of the person they replaced. I'm not sure it would last, but it's a few more years of good pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an evening course in building control, that's the inspection side, maybe two years part-time. I'd ask Brightline for days instead of nights so I could study, and I'd put aside something every month, even if it's small. I'd use the AI tools more, properly, because the inspectors will be using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a useful way. Like the week before an exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the course on what you've got?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd need the union or the government to help. I looked once, it's a few thousand. Priya would say do it and we'll eat pasta, and she'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're second wave with new things. Would you still wait for others here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not with five years. That's the difference. With the laser level I could wait a week. With this, if I wait two years, the course places are gone.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years and mustn't waste them like we did with climate change. I'd push in the union for retraining money and rules on how fast robots come in, and post about solutions rather than doom.
S3.think: Privately five years gives me a real chance to get ahead of it. With a building inspection qualification by thirty-two I'd be checking the robots' work, though I'm not sure how long that would last.
S3.do: Signs up for a two-year part-time evening course in building control and asks Brightline for day shifts so she can study. Saves a small amount each month and uses AI tools more seriously.
S3.feel: Anxious in a useful way, like the week before an exam.
S3.quote: With the laser level I could wait a week. With this, if I wait two years, the course places are gone.
S3.fieldNote: Five years changes Carla's habits: she says she'd stop waiting for others and move early. Her plan is concrete, but it depends on help with course fees. She treats the pressure as motivation rather than dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's more like my dad's world, where you had time to see things coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, so let's plan it like grown-ups: training, a proper safety net, and robots owned in ways that share the gains. I'd probably get more active in the union, maybe go to the regional meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is long enough that I'd be fine for most of it. I'd be thirty-seven when it hits, with a qualification and some experience in inspection or site management. The end point still worries me, because nobody's told me what anyone does when the machines do nearly everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the building control course, but slower, maybe over three years so I'm not exhausted. I'd keep working at Brightline and try to save. I'd want Priya and me to have the baby sooner rather than later, honestly, before it all lands, while I've still got a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than anxious. It's far enough away to plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's interesting, you'd bring the baby forward. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years I can see the window. If we wait until thirty-five, the robots might be here and I might be out of work. Better to have a toddler while I still have a payslip. Priya would laugh at me for planning it like a job schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it goes badly, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who had ten years and did nothing. Politicians who wait for it to be a crisis before they act. We'd have warning, so there's no excuse this time.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, with training, a proper safety net and robots owned in ways that share the gains. I'd get more active in the union and go to regional meetings.
S4.think: Privately I think I'd be fine for most of the decade and would be thirty-seven with a qualification when it hits. The end point still worries me, because nobody has said what people do afterwards.
S4.do: Takes the building control course more slowly over three years while working at Brightline. Saves where she can and plans with Priya to have a baby sooner, while she still has a wage.
S4.feel: Uneasy rather than anxious, because it's far enough away to plan around.
S4.quote: Better to have a toddler while I still have a payslip.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Carla thinks like a planner, even about family. She would bring a baby forward to fit the window while she still has a wage. Blame here goes to politicians who would have warning and still fail to act.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Five or ten I can plan for, two I just get hit by. What would help is a real income while you retrain, not some token amount, and courses you can do around shifts. And the union having enough members that the bosses actually have to talk to us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about women in the trade. It took me years to be taken seriously on site, and I'd hate to be first out because I'm not one of the lads. When jobs get scarce, that stuff comes back.

headlineQuote: It took me years to be taken seriously on site, and I'd hate to be first out because I'm not one of the lads.
portrait: Carla Diaz is a 27-year-old fit-out carpenter who builds shop and café interiors on night shifts for a small shopfitting firm, living with her nurse girlfriend Priya on about three weeks of savings. She learns new tools in the second wave, after someone else has proved them, and uses AI now and then. She is calm about the plateau, uneasy about losing half her work in the steady picture, and alarmed at AGI in two years. With five or ten years she'd move early, study building inspection and even bring a baby forward while she still has a wage.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she can plan for five or ten years but would simply be hit by two.
whatWouldHelp: A real income while retraining, courses that fit around shifts, and a union with enough members that employers have to negotiate.
